Consider short-term tocolysis where indicated to complete steroids/transfer, excluding infection or fetal compromise.
Early neonatology consultation and maternal transfer if a higher-level unit is needed.
management.safety: Tocolysis is not appropriate in chorioamnionitis, severe abruption or maternal/fetal deterioration.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 2-hour-old infant of a mother with diabetes is jittery and intermittently apnoeic. Bedside glucose is 1.5 mmol/L. The baby is too drowsy to breastfeed safely.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Commence insulin infusion because maternal diabetes makes neonatal glucose high.
Wait for formal laboratory confirmation without intervention.
Give oral glucose gel only and review in six hours.
Discharge because newborn glucose commonly falls in the first hours.
Provide immediate IV glucose according to neonatal emergency protocol and assess breathing and glucose response.
explanations: Postnatal hyperinsulinaemia causes hypoglycaemia; insulin would worsen it.
Severe symptomatic bedside hypoglycaemia needs immediate rescue while confirming laboratory value.
Symptomatic severe hypoglycaemia with impaired feeding requires IV treatment and close monitoring.
Symptoms and low glucose are dangerous and not a benign transitional finding.
Correct: neurological/respiratory symptoms mandate rapid parenteral correction.
pearl: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia is an emergency; treat immediately and look for persistent hyperinsulinism or infection if recurrent.
pivot: An asymptomatic newborn with milder low glucose may receive feeding plus glucose gel under an approved screening algorithm.

steps: Airway/breathing support as needed, temperature control, urgent IV access and blood sampling if it will not delay treatment.
IV dextrose bolus/infusion per neonatal protocol, then frequent glucose checks.
Feed/expressed milk once safe and titrate dextrose to maintain target glucose.
Review maternal diabetes, infection, prematurity and persistent hyperinsulinaemia.
management.safety: Repeated untreated hypoglycaemia risks neurological injury; check infusion concentration and access carefully.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 21-year-old has four days of unilateral severe sore throat, fever, muffled 'hot potato' voice and difficulty opening his mouth. Uvula deviates away from a bulging tonsillar pillar; he can handle secretions and oxygenation is normal.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Use inhaled salbutamol as first-line to treat the altered voice.
Give routine antiviral medication only and discharge.
Treat solely with oral antihistamine for presumed allergic oedema.
Perform elective tonsillectomy without assessing infection or hydration.
Urgent ENT review for drainage plus antibiotics and analgesia after airway assessment.
explanations: Upper oropharyngeal pathology does not respond to bronchodilator.
The unilateral fluctuant tonsillar swelling and uvular deviation point to bacterial abscess rather than HSV.
Fever, trismus and uvular deviation are not typical allergy.
Acute abscess care is immediate assessment, antibiotics, drainage; surgery is selective.
Correct: classic peritonsillar abscess requires drainage assessment and antimicrobial coverage.
pearl: Trismus, unilateral tonsillar swelling and uvular deviation distinguish peritonsillar abscess from uncomplicated pharyngitis.
pivot: Drooling, stridor, tripod posture or inability to handle secretions suggests dangerous airway infection and changes priorities.

steps: Check voice, stridor, drooling and ability to swallow; summon senior airway help if threatened.
Analgesia, hydration, appropriate oral/IV antibiotics and ENT assessment.
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage where indicated by trained clinician.
Ensure oral intake, improvement and return precautions; consider recurrent tonsillitis history.
management.safety: Never attempt forceful examination or drainage with an unsecured airway.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 39-year-old taking clozapine 350 mg daily has had no bowel movement for six days, increasing abdominal distension and vomiting. HR is 126/min, abdomen is tender and bowel sounds are absent.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Increase clozapine to improve psychotic symptoms before evaluating the abdomen.
Urgent hospital assessment for clozapine-associated gastrointestinal hypomotility/ileus; withhold clozapine pending specialist review.
Advise extra fibre alone and a routine clinic review next week.
Reassure because constipation is common and therefore harmless on clozapine.
Give loperamide to reduce vomiting-related diarrhoea risk.
explanations: Clozapine worsens gut hypomotility; escalation is unsafe.
Correct: GI hypomotility can progress to obstruction and fatal ischaemia; emergency surgical evaluation is needed.
Severe symptoms may indicate ileus/obstruction where fibre alone can worsen distension.
High prevalence does not mean safety; red flags demand urgent care.
Antimotility drugs worsen obstruction and are not indicated.
pearl: Clozapine gastrointestinal hypomotility may be more dangerous than agranulocytosis; actively ask about bowel motions every review.
pivot: Mild constipation without alarm signs requires proactive laxative regimen and monitoring before it progresses.

steps: No stools/flatus, severe pain, distension, vomiting, systemic toxicity; check vitals.
ED/surgery and psychiatry, abdominal imaging and IV fluids as appropriate; review/withhold clozapine.
Surgical or medical decompression according to cause; avoid blind laxatives until obstruction evaluated.
Bowel chart, regular prophylactic laxatives when appropriate, dietary/hydration measures and medication review.
management.safety: Do not use bulking agents when ileus/obstruction is suspected.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 50-year-old receiving red-cell transfusion develops abrupt fever 39.4°C, lumbar pain, hypotension and dark urine 15 minutes into the unit. She had been stable before transfusion.
ask: Which is the BEST first response?
options: Discharge once back pain improves.
Slow transfusion rate and reassess temperature after 20 minutes.
Stop transfusion, maintain IV access with normal saline, summon help and notify blood bank immediately.
Give paracetamol and continue the same unit.
Start a new red-cell unit from the same batch without checking identity.
explanations: Shock and haemoglobinuria can lead to DIC and AKI requiring monitoring.
Possible acute haemolytic transfusion reaction requires stopping blood immediately.
Correct: stop suspected incompatible blood, support ABC and initiate transfusion-reaction investigation.
Antipyretics alone cannot prevent ongoing haemolysis and shock.
Potential mismatched product must be investigated before further transfusion.
pearl: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction commonly presents early with fever, pain, hypotension and dark urine; immediately stop blood.
pivot: Isolated mild urticaria without systemic symptoms may permit a different graded response under transfusion policy.

steps: Stop blood, keep IV access with saline, verify patient/product identity and notify blood bank.
ABCDE, oxygen if needed, manage shock and monitor urine output.
Send appropriate pre/post samples, urine, haemolysis markers, coagulation and returned bag/tubing.
Document reaction and communicate safe future compatibility requirements.
management.safety: Never resume a suspected severe haemolytic reaction unit.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 76-year-old arrives with palpitations and near-syncope. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 190/min. BP is 68/40 mmHg, she is pale and intermittently confused; there is no evidence of pulmonary oedema.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate treatment?
options: Give IV metoprolol first and repeat until the heart rate is below 100/min.
Give intravenous digoxin and reassess in six hours.
Start oral anticoagulation and plan elective cardioversion in three weeks.
Give intravenous amiodarone and wait for conversion before summoning help.
Perform urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion with resuscitation support; sedate if feasible without delaying.
explanations: Beta blockade can worsen profound hypotension; this patient is haemodynamically unstable.
Digoxin is relatively slow and not an appropriate definitive first intervention in an unstable patient.
Anticoagulation planning matters but must not delay life-saving stabilisation of an unstable tachyarrhythmia.
Pharmacological rhythm control is too slow to be relied on in profound shock; call skilled support now.
Correct: shock and altered consciousness caused by a rapid tachyarrhythmia mandate immediate synchronised cardioversion.
pearl: Instability (shock, chest pain, pulmonary oedema, altered mentation) changes AF management from rate/risk planning to immediate synchronised cardioversion.
pivot: If stable, decide rate versus rhythm control and stroke prevention using duration, comorbidities, and anticoagulation considerations.

steps: Call resuscitation help, monitoring, IV access and check for precipitants such as sepsis, ischaemia or electrolyte derangement.
Deliver synchronised DC cardioversion with appropriate energy and sedation where feasible, without delaying treatment for profound shock.
Recheck ECG and BP; treat triggers and discuss anticoagulation and longer-term rhythm strategy.
management.safety: Ensure synchronisation for a tachyarrhythmia with a pulse; pulseless arrest uses the unsynchronised arrest algorithm.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 31-year-old at 29 weeks has gestational diabetes diagnosed by 75-g OGTT. She has started a diet and walking plan. Her past week's pre-breakfast values are repeatedly 5.8–6.3 mmol/L, while post-meal readings are largely within local targets; fetal growth is appropriate.
ask: What is the BEST next step?
options: Begin an individualized pharmacological plan, often basal insulin, alongside ongoing lifestyle advice and glucose monitoring.
Induce labour immediately at 29 weeks because any fasting hyperglycaemia endangers the fetus.
Stop home glucose checks and use HbA1c at term to assess control.
Advise carbohydrate elimination and prolonged fasting to normalise fasting glucose.
Continue diet alone for six more weeks despite consistently above-target fasting readings.
explanations: Correct: persistently high fasting readings despite lifestyle change suggest need for overnight basal glucose-lowering treatment.
A mildly persistent fasting elevation alone does not warrant extremely preterm delivery.
HbA1c does not replace pregnancy-specific glucose profiles for short-term treatment adjustment.
Severe caloric/carbohydrate restriction is inappropriate in pregnancy and can risk ketosis and nutritional deficiency.
Persistently elevated fasting glucose warrants treatment review sooner because fetal exposure continues.
pearl: Fasting hyperglycaemia often needs basal insulin; postprandial excursions may need meal-specific therapy. Pregnancy targets are more stringent.
pivot: If readings are at target on lifestyle treatment, continue nutrition/activity counselling and growth surveillance without immediate medication.

steps: Review actual glucometer log, meal timing, overnight snacks, technique and local fasting/post-meal targets.
Refer diabetes-in-pregnancy team and introduce medication (often basal insulin) when repeated fasting values remain above target; teach hypoglycaemia safety if insulin started.
Continue pre-breakfast and post-meal checks, dose titration, fetal growth assessment and postpartum diabetes re-screening plan.
management.safety: Metformin/insulin choices depend on local pregnancy policy, contraindications and shared decision-making; avoid extrapolating non-pregnant glucose targets.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 73-year-old has fever 39.5 °C, jaundice, RUQ pain and hypotension. Bilirubin is 110 µmol/L, ALT elevated and ultrasound shows a 12 mm common bile duct with suspected distal stone.
ask: Which intervention should be prioritised once resuscitation begins?
options: Give oral ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve the duct stone.
Observe on IV antibiotics alone until fever resolves, regardless of persistent obstruction.
Perform laparoscopic cholecystectomy alone before treating the obstructed duct.
Repeat ultrasound next month because duct dilation is often age related.
Provide urgent biliary decompression, usually ERCP, in addition to IV antibiotics and shock resuscitation.
explanations: This does not provide rapid drainage or infection control.
Antibiotics alone may fail when infected bile remains obstructed and needs source control.
Gallbladder removal will not urgently drain an infected obstructed CBD in shock.
Charcot triad plus shock indicates severe cholangitis needing urgent source control.
Correct: severe cholangitis requires early antimicrobial therapy and urgent biliary drainage.
pearl: Ascending cholangitis = infection behind biliary obstruction. Definitive management is source control by duct drainage.
pivot: Uncomplicated symptomatic cholelithiasis without cholangitis is managed with elective/early cholecystectomy rather than emergency ERCP.

steps: ABCDE, IV access, cultures, fluids with reassessment and vasopressors if septic shock persists.
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative bacteria and appropriate enterococci according to local policy.
Urgent gastroenterology/ERCP for biliary stent or stone extraction; percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP unavailable/failed.
Arrange definitive gallstone management to reduce recurrence.
management.safety: Do not wait for full normalisation of LFTs or cultures before arranging drainage in severe cholangitis.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 79-year-old two days after hip surgery is disorientated, sees insects on the wall and alternates between drowsiness and agitation over hours. He was cognitively intact before admission. He has a urinary catheter and received opioids overnight.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate first management strategy?
options: Diagnose schizophrenia and commence a long-term antipsychotic plan.
Ignore confusion because postoperative hallucinations always resolve without complication.
Treat possible precipitants and provide orientation, sleep, sensory aids and safe supervision; use short-term medication only if severe distress/risk.
Administer high-dose benzodiazepines routinely as first line for all delirium.
Obtain a psychiatric inpatient transfer before checking vital signs or glucose.
explanations: Sudden onset with fluctuating attention following illness/surgery indicates delirium, not a chronic primary psychosis.
Delirium can indicate infection, drug toxicity, hypoxia or metabolic illness and predicts adverse outcomes.
Correct: delirium care prioritises identifying causes, non-drug measures and cautious symptom management.
Benzodiazepines often worsen non-withdrawal delirium and carry respiratory/fall risks.
Immediate medical assessment for reversible precipitants is essential.
pearl: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention/awareness; always seek medical precipitants and medication effects.
pivot: Gradual progressive cognitive decline without fluctuation suggests dementia, although dementia also increases delirium vulnerability.

steps: Assess ABC, oxygenation, glucose, pain, urine retention, constipation, infection and medication toxicity.
Reorientation, hearing aids/glasses, family presence, day-night routine, mobility, hydration and minimisation of unnecessary catheters.
Supervised low-dose antipsychotic only for severe distress/behavioural risk after non-drug measures and QT/Parkinson risk review.
Monitor daily for resolution and communicate cognitive baseline to carers.
management.safety: Avoid antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia or Parkinsonism unless senior specialist-directed; check QT risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 24-year-old returns from a camping trip in a tick-endemic region. He has fever, severe headache, myalgia and a petechial rash involving wrists, ankles, palms and soles. He is stable but appears unwell; serological tests are pending.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give oral acyclovir as the sole therapy.
Treat with topical corticosteroid until rash resolves.
Prescribe amoxicillin as guaranteed first-line treatment for all rickettsial species.
Give empiric doxycycline promptly while obtaining appropriate diagnostic tests.
Await a positive serology before starting medication.
explanations: The pattern and tick exposure support rickettsial disease rather than isolated HSV.
A systemic febrile vasculitic infection needs systemic antibiotics.
Beta-lactams are not reliably effective against intracellular rickettsiae.
Correct: compatible severe tick-borne rickettsiosis should be treated empirically.
Early serology may be negative and delayed treatment in rickettsial infection worsens outcomes.
pearl: For suspected severe rickettsial infection, start doxycycline based on clinical features and exposure, not confirmatory serology.
pivot: If meningism, shock or severe thrombocytopenia predominates, evaluate other life-threatening infections and co-infections concurrently.

steps: Travel/activity timeline, tick exposure, exam rash and eschar, vitals, organ dysfunction.
Start empiric doxycycline after reviewing contraindications and regional guidance; do not wait for early serology.
Send PCR/serology as locally appropriate, monitor platelet count, sodium and renal/liver function.
Admit if hypotension, hypoxaemia or neurological changes develop.
management.safety: Doxycycline is recommended even for children with serious suspected rickettsioses; expert/local guidance governs dosing.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 22-year-old at 10 weeks gestation has vomited frequently for three weeks and lost 8% of her booking weight. She has ketonuria, hypokalaemia and dehydration; she has eaten almost nothing. She is admitted for IV fluids and antiemetics.
ask: Which addition is particularly important before giving glucose-containing IV fluids?
options: Oral iron tablets before rehydration.
Intravenous vitamin K to prevent early pregnancy bleeding.
Long-term corticosteroids as the only antiemetic.
Routine high-dose vitamin A supplementation.
Parenteral thiamine to reduce the risk of Wernicke encephalopathy.
explanations: Iron can worsen nausea and does not prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Vitamin K is not the key immediate deficiency in prolonged vomiting.
Steroids may be reserved for refractory symptoms but do not address immediate thiamine risk.
Excess vitamin A is teratogenic and does not address the immediate nutritional risk.
Correct: prolonged vomiting and poor intake can deplete thiamine, and glucose may precipitate Wernicke in deficient patients.
pearl: In prolonged hyperemesis, give thiamine before or with carbohydrate-containing fluids; do not delay treatment of true hypoglycaemia.
pivot: If vomiting is mild without weight loss, dehydration or electrolyte problems, dietary changes and oral antiemetics may suffice.

steps: Clinical hydration, weight loss, electrolytes, renal function, nutrition and alternative causes of vomiting.
IV isotonic fluids with potassium as appropriate; parenteral thiamine before dextrose when feasible.
Stepwise pregnancy-appropriate antiemetics and nutritional support; monitor for refeeding risk.
Track urine output, weight and electrolytes; arrange follow-up and psychological support.
management.safety: Any confusion, nystagmus or ataxia raises concern for Wernicke encephalopathy requiring urgent high-dose parenteral thiamine.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 16-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia presents with vomiting, dehydration and collapse. Na is 119 mmol/L, K 7.1 mmol/L, glucose 2.9 mmol/L and BP 52/30 mmHg. There is no family history.
ask: Which initial management is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform elective genetic counselling as the only immediate intervention.
Give oral spironolactone to reduce potassium and review tomorrow.
Administer emergency parenteral hydrocortisone, isotonic fluids and treat hypoglycaemia/hyperkalaemia with monitoring.
Start prophylactic oral antibiotics alone for presumed gastroenteritis.
Delay treatment pending 17-hydroxyprogesterone laboratory confirmation.
explanations: Counselling is valuable later; immediate endocrine resuscitation comes first.
Potassium-sparing diuretics worsen hyperkalaemia and this infant is in shock.
Correct: salt-wasting CAH can produce fatal adrenal crisis requiring steroids and resuscitation.
Vomiting does not explain the profound salt loss, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia.
Testing must not delay life-saving adrenal-crisis therapy.
pearl: A vomiting neonate with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and shock requires adrenal insufficiency consideration.
pivot: Isolated ambiguous genitalia without salt loss still warrants endocrine evaluation but not automatic shock resuscitation.

steps: ABCDE, glucose, IV/IO access, ECG and close K/BP monitoring.
Emergency hydrocortisone and cautious isotonic saline; correct glucose and severe potassium as indicated.
17-OHP, electrolytes, renin and endocrine/genetic studies without delaying treatment.
Endocrine management including maintenance hormones and parent sick-day/emergency injection teaching.
management.safety: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes additionally requires immediate myocardial protection.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 48-year-old notices a sudden severe hearing loss in the right ear on waking 18 hours ago. Otoscopy is normal, Rinne is positive bilaterally and Weber lateralises to the left. No vertigo or focal neurological deficit is reported.
ask: What is the BEST next management?
options: Wait one month because sudden unilateral loss is usually wax.
Recommend hearing aids only without investigating the onset.
Start antibiotic ear drops for presumed otitis externa.
Arrange same-day ENT/audiology assessment with prompt corticosteroid treatment consideration.
Arrange elective grommet insertion.
explanations: Normal otoscopy and tuning forks indicate sensorineural loss, not impacted cerumen.
Rehabilitation may follow, but acute potentially salvageable hearing loss needs urgent assessment.
No ear canal inflammation or conductive findings support otitis externa.
Correct: sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a time-sensitive otological emergency.
Middle-ear ventilation tubes treat selected conductive conditions, not sudden inner-ear loss.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss warrants urgent referral, ideally within 24 hours, because early treatment improves recovery chances.
pivot: Unilateral hearing loss with pain/effusion and a negative Rinne suggests conductive disease needing a different pathway.

steps: History and examination, otoscopy, tuning forks, neurologic screen and audiogram.
ENT assessment for oral or intratympanic steroids based on contraindications/time window.
Consider MRI internal auditory canals to exclude retrocochlear cause after urgent treatment planning.
Repeat audiometry and hearing rehabilitation if deficit persists.
management.safety: Stroke symptoms, vertigo with neurological signs or facial weakness require emergency neurological assessment.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 31-year-old has recurrent episodes of palpitations, tremor and intense fear lasting ten minutes. Today she reports similar symptoms plus persistent chest pain and unilateral calf swelling after a long flight. HR 122/min and SpO2 93%.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate approach?
options: Start long-term benzodiazepine therapy and discharge.
Perform urgent assessment for pulmonary embolism and other cardiopulmonary causes before attributing symptoms to panic.
Diagnose panic disorder and prescribe an SSRI without further assessment.
Perform a routine psychiatric personality inventory and review next month.
Offer breathing exercises as sole treatment, since recurrent attacks prove a functional cause.
explanations: Sedation can mask deterioration, and long-term benzodiazepines are not preferred panic maintenance therapy.
Correct: potentially dangerous medical mimics must be excluded using history, vital signs and appropriate investigation.
Chest pain, hypoxaemia and thromboembolic clues require medical assessment first.
Immediate physiology and VTE risk take priority.
A previous panic diagnosis never excludes an acute medical illness.
pearl: Panic symptoms overlap with arrhythmia, PE, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia and stimulant effects.
pivot: If repeated episodes have normal focused medical assessment and expected panic features, CBT and SSRIs may be offered.

steps: ABCDE, ECG, glucose, oxygenation and assess chest pain/leg findings.
PE probability pathway and ECG/troponin when indicated rather than universal testing.
Explain panic physiology, initiate CBT and consider SSRI; avoid reinforcing repeated unnecessary testing.
Return urgently for syncope, persistent chest pain or new breathlessness.
management.safety: Never attribute abnormal vital signs to anxiety by default.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 58-year-old with chronic venous insufficiency has rapid onset of tender, sharply demarcated bright-red erythema on one shin with temperature 38.1°C. No bullae or necrosis, pain is proportionate, BP normal, lactate normal.
ask: What is the BEST initial management?
options: Urgent wide fascial debridement for every sharply bordered erythema.
Treat suspected streptococcal erysipelas with appropriate systemic antibiotics and early clinical reassessment.
Give oral prednisolone as sole therapy.
Delay therapy until blood cultures turn positive.
Prescribe topical antifungal alone because infection in venous legs is always fungal.
explanations: Features fit uncomplicated erysipelas without deep necrotising signs.
Correct: sharply raised demarcation and systemic fever suggest superficial dermal streptococcal infection.
Steroids do not eradicate infection and can worsen untreated cellulitis.
Cultures may be negative; uncomplicated erysipelas is diagnosed clinically.
Acute unilateral hot painful erythema with fever requires systemic treatment.
pearl: Erysipelas is a superficial streptococcal skin infection with sharply defined raised borders; look for portals such as tinea pedis.
pivot: Disproportionate pain, bullae, crepitus or shock suggests deeper necrotising infection requiring immediate surgery.

steps: Vitals and risk factors, borders, abscess, necrosis, immune state and glycaemic control.
Appropriate narrow-spectrum anti-streptococcal antibiotic adjusted for allergy and severity, limb elevation and analgesia.
Treat toe-web fungal disease, oedema/skin breaks; reassess response in 24–48h.
Admit for toxicity, progression or failure of oral therapy.
management.safety: Consider DVT or stasis dermatitis if clinical features diverge.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 68-year-old with advanced CKD presents with weakness. Potassium is 7.2 mmol/L and ECG shows broad QRS complexes and tall tented T waves. She is conscious with BP 122/80 mmHg.
ask: What is the BEST first drug to administer?
options: Give a potassium-binding agent alone and arrange routine outpatient review.
Administer insulin without glucose to produce a faster potassium fall.
Give IV furosemide alone irrespective of volume status.
Administer IV calcium under ECG monitoring immediately, then shift and eliminate potassium.
Give nebulised salbutamol alone and check potassium in one hour.
explanations: Binders are too slow to rescue an ECG-toxic hyperkalaemia emergency.
Insulin is paired with glucose and close glucose monitoring; initial IV calcium is the most immediate step for ECG changes.
Diuresis is unreliable in advanced CKD and cannot rapidly stabilise an abnormal ECG.
Correct: ECG changes indicate myocardial toxicity; IV calcium stabilises cardiac membranes before potassium-lowering drugs take effect.
Salbutamol can shift potassium into cells, but it does not immediately stabilise a threatened myocardium.
pearl: Calcium protects the heart but does not remove potassium; insulin–glucose, beta agonist and dialysis strategies must follow.
pivot: If severe hyperkalaemia has no ECG changes, urgent potassium shifting and elimination remain essential, with calcium guided by protocols and clinical risk.

steps: Continuous ECG; assess ABC, IV access, recheck non-haemolysed sample without delaying rescue for convincing ECG changes.
Give appropriate IV calcium formulation/dose per protocol and repeat if ECG changes persist; monitor IV site and rhythm.
Give IV insulin with glucose and consider nebulised salbutamol; check glucose repeatedly for delayed hypoglycaemia.
Stop contributors; discuss urgent dialysis for refractory severe hyperkalaemia or kidney failure; trend K and ECG for rebound.
management.safety: Do not confuse 10% calcium chloride and 10% calcium gluconate doses; follow your exact product and local resuscitation guideline.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A well 38-week infant aged 40 hours has increasing jaundice. TSB is above the gestation- and age-specific intensive-phototherapy threshold but below exchange threshold; feeding is modestly reduced. Blood group incompatibility is possible.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Initiate intensive phototherapy with hydration and haemolysis evaluation and serial bilirubin checks.
Perform immediate exchange transfusion for any bilirubin above the phototherapy line.
Arrange outpatient review in a week because jaundice is physiologic under 48 hours.
Stop breastfeeding permanently to reduce bilirubin production.
Give oral phenobarbital as sole therapy and repeat bilirubin the next day.
explanations: Correct: manage against hour/gestation/risk-specific thresholds, evaluate cause and track response.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for much higher levels or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy per protocol.
Threshold-exceeding hyperbilirubinaemia can cause neurotoxicity and needs prompt therapy irrespective of being early.
Support effective feeding; routine permanent breastfeeding cessation is not appropriate.
Phenobarbital is not standard immediate first-line for potentially hazardous early neonatal bilirubin rise.
pearl: Treat neonatal bilirubin using postnatal hours, gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors, not a fixed 'yellow colour' threshold.
pivot: If the bilirubin reaches exchange threshold or neurological signs appear, escalate urgently to neonatal exchange-transfusion pathway.

steps: Confirm TSB and chart against correct local nomogram; examine hydration, stool/urine, lethargy and neurological signs.
Start intensive phototherapy without delay; support enteral feeding/expressed milk and fluids as clinically indicated.
Maternal/baby blood groups and DAT where indicated, FBC/reticulocytes, haemolysis/G6PD assessment based on risk and jaundice onset.
Repeat TSB at recommended intervals, measure rebound if risk factors, arrange neonatal follow-up.
management.safety: Exchange transfusion requires senior neonatology and specialised preparation; never delay escalation in acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 25-year-old at 22 weeks gestation develops migratory periumbilical-to-right lower quadrant pain, focal tenderness and low-grade fever. Ultrasound cannot visualise the appendix. Maternal vitals are stable and fetal heart rate is present.
ask: What is the NEXT most appropriate step?
options: Obtain MRI abdomen/pelvis without gadolinium and involve surgery/obstetrics.
Give opioid analgesia then postpone evaluation until after delivery.
Perform immediate laparotomy without review or additional assessment solely because ultrasound was inconclusive.
Discharge because pregnancy-related ligament pain explains right-sided discomfort.
Perform urgent contrast CT in every pregnant woman before senior review.
explanations: Correct: after non-diagnostic ultrasound in a stable pregnant patient, MRI is a useful non-ionising diagnostic test.
Analgesia should not delay evaluation of potential surgical abdomen.
The clinical picture and availability of MRI/senior surgical review guide timing; a stable case allows rapid diagnostic refinement.
Progressive focal pain and fever raise appendicitis concern; delayed diagnosis risks perforation.
CT can be used when necessary but is not automatically preferred when MRI is available and the patient stable.
pearl: In pregnancy, appendicitis can have atypical anatomy; diagnostic delay raises perforation and preterm labour risk.
pivot: If generalised peritonitis or maternal instability is present, urgent surgery may supersede further imaging.

steps: Senior obstetric and general surgery assessment, maternal observations, abdominal exam and fetal assessment.
Ultrasound first; MRI without gadolinium if non-diagnostic and available, or CT when clinically indicated and benefits outweigh radiation risk.
IV antibiotics and timely appendicectomy under surgical/anaesthetic planning, with perioperative fetal considerations.
management.safety: Do not withhold necessary surgery because of pregnancy; delay may pose a greater risk.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 35-year-old woman attends GP repeatedly for abdominal pain. Her partner answers every question and refuses to leave. When seen briefly alone she reveals he controls her money and has threatened to hurt her if she leaves. She asks that no details be disclosed to him.
ask: What is the BEST initial response?
options: Tell her she must leave the relationship today and contact police without discussing her preferences.
Call the partner into the room to confront him and explain why threats are unacceptable.
Treat pain only and avoid discussing the threats because this is a non-medical issue.
Arrange a private, trauma-informed safety assessment, document objectively and discuss safe referral and disclosure limits.
Promise absolute confidentiality even if there is imminent danger to a child or another person.
explanations: A blanket directive can increase risk; mandatory reporting/legal duties depend on local law and specific risks.
Confrontation can increase immediate danger, especially with coercive control.
Family violence has direct medical and safety consequences and deserves compassionate clinical response.
Correct: respect autonomy, confidentiality and immediate safety while offering specialist supports.
Confidentiality has legally defined limits in serious safety situations; explain these honestly.
pearl: Coercive control is a serious form of abuse; ask privately, check immediate danger and avoid actions that may increase retaliation.
pivot: If a child is at risk or imminent serious harm exists, statutory safeguarding duties may justify limited disclosures under local law.

steps: See the patient without partner; ask whether it is safe to talk and which communication channels are safe.
Immediate threats, weapons, strangulation, escalation, children/dependents and safe place to go; seek emergency help if imminent danger.
Validate disclosure without judgement, offer domestic-violence service contacts, safe documentation and follow-up.
Explain confidentiality and statutory disclosure obligations; avoid printing unsafe messages or sending alerts to shared devices.
management.safety: Never assume that 'just leave' is a safe intervention; departure can be a period of increased risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A tall 23-year-old experiences sudden pleuritic right chest pain. CXR shows a moderate right pneumothorax with no mediastinal shift. SpO2 98% room air, BP 120/76 mmHg, RR 20/min and pain is controlled. He has no lung disease and no breathlessness at rest.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Start prophylactic antibiotics because pneumothorax is invariably infectious.
Immediately perform emergency needle decompression for suspected tension physiology.
Insert a large-bore chest drain in every pneumothorax irrespective of stability.
Prescribe systemic corticosteroids to re-expand the lung.
Provide conservative symptom-led management with observation/follow-up where appropriate under local spontaneous pneumothorax guidance.
explanations: A spontaneous primary pneumothorax is not typically a bacterial infection.
He has no shock or significant respiratory compromise; needle decompression is reserved for tension pneumothorax.
Invasive drainage is not mandatory for every uncomplicated primary pneumothorax.
Steroids do not remove pleural air.
Correct: a stable minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax may be observed without intervention when criteria and follow-up are met.
pearl: Treat spontaneous pneumothorax based on symptoms, stability, underlying disease and safe follow-up—not radiographic size alone.
pivot: Secondary pneumothorax in COPD or significant breathlessness has a lower threshold for drainage/admission.

steps: Assess breathlessness, pain, oxygenation, haemodynamic stability and known lung disease.
Stable minimally symptomatic primary cases may be managed conservatively; more symptomatic cases may need aspiration or drain.
Clear return precautions, avoid air travel until radiographic resolution and discuss recurrence/smoking cessation.
Arrange appropriate clinical and radiographic review, and surgical advice for recurrent/persistent leaks.
management.safety: Any evolving tension physiology overrides the conservative pathway.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 31-year-old singleton pregnancy at 19+5 weeks has a prior spontaneous preterm birth at 28 weeks. Transvaginal cervical length on routine surveillance is 18 mm; membranes are intact and there are no contractions, bleeding or infection signs.
ask: Which intervention is MOST appropriate to discuss urgently?
options: Start prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics for the remainder of pregnancy.
Offer only bed rest for two months as proven first-line prevention.
Schedule a cervical cerclage assessment, with progesterone and surveillance decisions individualised by history and protocol.
Recommend immediate delivery to avoid intrauterine infection.
Perform abdominal CT to exclude cervical cancer before treatment.
explanations: No evidence of infection; prolonged antibiotics do not treat mechanical cervical risk.
Routine bed rest has not shown reliable benefit and has harms.
Correct: prior spontaneous preterm birth with short cervix before 24 weeks is a classic scenario for ultrasound-indicated cerclage discussion.
There is no labour, infection or indication for pregnancy termination.
CT offers no role in this obstetric short-cervix management.
pearl: Cerclage eligibility depends on prior preterm birth, measured cervical length, singleton status and gestational age.
pivot: If membranes are ruptured, active contractions, bleeding or infection occurs, cerclage may be contraindicated.

steps: Review obstetric history, transvaginal measurement, membrane status and exclusion of contractions/infection.
Urgent consultant review for cerclage before gestational threshold; review vaginal progesterone and local pathways.
Explain procedural risks, need for symptom vigilance and ongoing cervical/pregnancy follow-up.
Seek urgent review for discharge of fluid, bleeding, fever or painful contractions.
management.safety: Cervical cerclage is not routine once membrane rupture or intra-amniotic infection is suspected.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 13-year-old admitted with DKA is receiving IV fluids and insulin per protocol. Four hours later she develops a new headache, bradycardia, increased BP and reduced conscious level. Blood glucose is falling gradually and sodium changes are being monitored.
ask: What is the BEST immediate action?
options: Stop all fluids completely and discharge when glucose normalises.
Give oral paracetamol and reassess after two hours.
Wait for CT head confirmation before intervening.
Increase insulin rate to clear ketones faster.
Treat presumptive DKA-related cerebral injury immediately with hyperosmolar therapy and PICU escalation.
explanations: She is unstable with potential neurological catastrophe; fluid management must be reviewed by experts.
Analgesia alone dangerously delays treatment of possible cerebral oedema.
Clinical signs of cerebral injury in DKA require treatment before imaging.
Aggressive insulin escalation may worsen osmotic complications and does not treat suspected cerebral oedema.
Correct: headache, bradycardia, hypertension and declining consciousness are classic warning signs.
pearl: Neurological deterioration during paediatric DKA treatment is presumed cerebral injury until proven otherwise.
pivot: A mild headache without neurological signs still needs careful serial assessment but not automatic hyperosmolar rescue.

steps: Call PICU and senior paediatrics immediately; ABC, neuro observations and head elevation.
Give hyperosmolar agent (mannitol or hypertonic saline) according to paediatric DKA cerebral-injury protocol without awaiting CT.
Reassess fluids, insulin, electrolytes, glucose and ventilation; avoid unnecessary hyperventilation.
CT/MRI when stabilised to assess differential causes.
management.safety: Do not delay cerebral-injury treatment for imaging.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 34-year-old after a fall has a deformed forearm with a 4 cm wound communicating with visible bone. Distal pulse and sensation are present, BP stable. There is gravel contamination.
ask: Which treatment sequence is MOST appropriate?
options: Give timely IV antibiotics/tetanus prophylaxis, cover and splint the limb and arrange urgent operative debridement.
Delay all intervention until formal CT angiography despite intact neurovascular examination.
Give oral antibiotics only and splint without surgery.
Irrigate in the ward until the wound looks clean, then omit antibiotics.
Close the skin tightly in ED then review in one week.
explanations: Correct: infection prevention begins immediately, with definitive surgery guided by fracture and wound severity.
Imaging may be helpful selectively but cannot delay antibiotics and wound care.
Open fractures usually need IV antibiotics, tetanus assessment and operative debridement/fixation.
Visual cleanliness does not exclude contamination; early systemic antibiotics matter.
Primary closure before formal irrigation/debridement can trap contamination.
pearl: Open fractures require early IV antibiotics, sterile coverage, neurovascular documentation and surgical source control.
pivot: A closed fracture without skin communication has different infection prophylaxis and operative urgency.

steps: Before/after splint, assess pulses, perfusion, motor and sensation; photograph according to consent/policy.
Remove gross debris only when appropriate, saline-moistened sterile cover, immobilise and treat pain.
Prompt IV antibiotics selected for grade and contamination, tetanus assessment.
Urgent orthopaedic/plastic assessment for debridement and stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not repeatedly probe the open wound or perform unplanned closure.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 28-year-old is found unresponsive with RR 5/min, pinpoint pupils and SpO2 75%. A syringe is nearby. A pulse is present; he responds only to painful stimulus.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate treatment?
options: Give a sedating antipsychotic for presumed agitation before checking breathing.
Wait for urine toxicology confirmation before giving any antidote.
Give flumazenil routinely to reverse opioid-related respiratory depression.
Provide airway/ventilation support and administer naloxone titrated to restoring adequate respiration.
Give oral activated charcoal to an unconscious patient without airway protection.
explanations: Further sedating medication may worsen the patient's dangerously slow breathing; immediate ventilation and naloxone take priority.
Clinical respiratory depression mandates immediate resuscitation.
Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with seizure risks, not opioid reversal.
Correct: ventilation is vital; naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression but may wear off before the opioid.
High aspiration risk and no role before life-saving airway management.
pearl: In opioid overdose the target is adequate ventilation, not forcing complete alertness at the cost of severe withdrawal.
pivot: If pulseless, initiate CPR and advanced life support while treating likely opioid cause.

steps: Call emergency help, airway manoeuvres, oxygen and bag-mask ventilation; monitor ECG and glucose.
Titrated naloxone IV/IM/intranasal per local pathway; repeat or infuse for long-acting opioids.
Watch for re-sedation, aspiration, pulmonary complications and precipitated withdrawal.
Offer overdose education, take-home naloxone and addiction support after recovery.
management.safety: Do not leave a patient unobserved once naloxone initially works.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 69-year-old experiences 12 minutes of left arm weakness and speech slurring, now completely resolved. BP 150/90 mmHg, irregularly irregular pulse 104/min and glucose normal. He has no headache or prior stroke.
ask: What is the BEST next step?
options: Wait for a second attack before neuroimaging.
Start long-term aspirin and warfarin together immediately without brain imaging or AF confirmation.
Arrange urgent same-day TIA/stroke assessment with vascular imaging, ECG and risk-directed antithrombotic plan.
Reassure because complete resolution excludes cerebral ischaemia.
Order outpatient EEG as the main investigation because transient signs imply seizure.
explanations: Early recurrent stroke risk is highest soon after TIA; waiting is unsafe.
Antithrombotic choice depends on imaging and source; empiric combination carries bleeding risk.
Correct: expedite aetiology and secondary prevention; atrial fibrillation is a possible cardioembolic source.
TIA is a warning of imminent stroke despite complete symptom resolution.
A focal negative neurological deficit with dysarthria suggests vascular event; seizure is differential but not first assumption.
pearl: Resolved focal deficit is a TIA emergency: evaluate rapidly and intervene on stroke mechanisms.
pivot: If MRI shows infarction, the event is tissue-positive stroke even if symptoms have resolved.

steps: Urgent specialist TIA/stroke pathway, document onset/duration and neurological findings.
Brain and vascular imaging per protocol, ECG for AF, BP, lipids, glucose and carotid disease.
Antiplatelet or anticoagulation according to mechanism/timing, statin and risk-factor management.
Return immediately for recurrent symptoms; driving and lifestyle guidance.
management.safety: Do not delay referral based solely on a low risk score.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 64-year-old is brought to the ED 50 minutes after sudden right-arm weakness and expressive aphasia. Blood glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. BP 174/92 mmHg and NIHSS is 12. He has no head injury.
ask: What is the BEST next investigation/action sequence?
options: Observe for 24 hours because the deficit might resolve spontaneously.
Order MRI brain routinely before assessing eligibility for reperfusion.
Activate stroke protocol with urgent non-contrast CT brain and vessel imaging as appropriate.
Perform lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage before any brain imaging.
Give aspirin immediately and arrange CT head only if neurological signs deteriorate.
explanations: Potentially reversible brain tissue is time dependent; waiting loses the reperfusion opportunity.
MRI can be useful in selected pathways, but routine MRI-first should not delay urgent CT-based assessment and reperfusion.
Correct: exclude haemorrhage immediately and assess IV thrombolysis and large-vessel thrombectomy eligibility within time windows.
LP is not first-line in classic acute focal ischaemic stroke and introduces dangerous delay.
Haemorrhage must be excluded before antithrombotic or reperfusion decisions; early aspirin may be unsafe.
pearl: Stroke treatments depend on time, imaging, premorbid function and contraindications; normal glucose helps exclude a mimic, not haemorrhage.
pivot: If symptoms have completely resolved, assess as TIA with urgent vascular/cardiac risk evaluation rather than dismissing the episode.

steps: Record last-known-well time, bedside glucose, focused neuro exam/NIHSS and anticoagulant history; call stroke team.
Immediate non-contrast CT to exclude bleed and CT angiography when indicated to assess proximal occlusion.
Determine thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy eligibility with BP and bleeding-risk screening; avoid empiric antiplatelets before exclusion of haemorrhage.
Swallow screen before oral intake, monitor BP, glucose and neuro status; secondary prevention after imaging and definitive treatment.
management.safety: Do not delay imaging while waiting for routine labs unless a specific safety issue dictates.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 4-month-old has 3 days of coryza and cough, diffuse fine crackles, RR 66/min, moderate recession, SpO2 89% in room air and only 40% of usual feeds over 12 hours. No focal findings suggest bacterial pneumonia.
ask: Which is the BEST treatment plan?
options: Give routine inhaled salbutamol and oral antibiotics as first-line treatment.
Start high-dose oral prednisolone for five days without oxygen therapy.
Obtain urgent CT chest before deciding whether respiratory support is needed.
Discharge with reassurance alone because bronchiolitis is self-limiting.
Admit for oxygen according to target, gentle nasal suction if obstructed, and hydration support.
explanations: Bronchiolitis is usually viral; routine bronchodilators and antibiotics do not improve outcomes.
Steroids are not routinely indicated in typical infant bronchiolitis and do not treat current hypoxaemia.
CT adds radiation and delay; bedside assessment guides immediate supportive care.
Hypoxaemia, feeding difficulty and respiratory effort require assessment/admission and support.
Correct: the key interventions are oxygenation, adequate fluid intake and monitoring work of breathing.
pearl: For bronchiolitis, supportive care is the treatment; escalating work of breathing, apnoea, exhaustion and poor feeding are danger signs.
pivot: In an older child with recurrent wheeze and a clear response to bronchodilator, consider viral-triggered asthma instead.

steps: RR, work of breathing, apnoea, hydration, perfusion, saturation and risk factors such as prematurity.
Give oxygen as local threshold requires, nasal saline/gentle suction if obstructed, smaller feeds or NG/IV fluids if oral intake inadequate.
Observe saturation, feeding and fatigue; high-flow nasal support/critical-care review for persistent hypoxaemia or exhaustion.
management.safety: Avoid unnecessary chest imaging, bronchodilators, antibiotics and systemic steroids in routine bronchiolitis.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 21-year-old three hours after tibial shaft fracture fixation has escalating leg pain despite opioids. Toes are warm and pulses palpable. Passive extension of the toes causes severe pain; calf compartments feel tense.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Elevate the limb well above heart level and use ice while waiting 12 hours.
Document palpable pulses and observe until the next ward round.
Request routine outpatient nerve conduction studies in six weeks.
Urgently notify orthopaedics, remove constrictive dressings and prepare for emergency fasciotomy.
Increase opioid analgesia and apply a tighter compressive dressing.
explanations: Marked elevation can worsen perfusion; suspected compartment syndrome requires immediate surgical evaluation.
Pulses often remain present early in compartment syndrome and do not exclude ischaemic damage.
Neuropathy testing is irrelevant and dangerously delayed for threatened muscle necrosis.
Correct: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch after trauma are classic signs needing urgent decompression.
Analgesia and compression mask or worsen dangerous compartment pressure.
pearl: Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical time-critical diagnosis; present pulses or normal skin colour do NOT rule it out.
pivot: If findings are equivocal in a sedated/unreliable patient, compartment pressure measurement may help, but must not delay treatment of obvious disease.

steps: Call orthopaedic surgeon immediately; check pain with passive stretch, sensation, motor function and compartment tension.
Split dressings/cast, keep limb near heart level, give oxygen/support BP and analgesia without delay.
Emergency surgical fasciotomy and postoperative monitoring for rhabdomyolysis, renal injury and wound complications.
management.safety: Delay can cause irreversible myonecrosis and nerve injury within hours.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: An 80-year-old taking apixaban for AF presents with melaena, BP 86/48 mmHg, Hb 69 g/L and ongoing haematemesis. Last apixaban dose was five hours ago. He is confused and cool peripherally.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate plan?
options: Hold apixaban, resuscitate/transfuse as needed and urgently discuss specific reversal plus endoscopic source control.
Continue apixaban to prevent stroke and arrange routine endoscopy in a week.
Give oral vitamin K because it rapidly reverses all direct oral anticoagulants.
Start therapeutic IV heparin as a bridge while awaiting endoscopy.
Arrange discharge on oral iron once the blood pressure transiently improves.
explanations: Correct: major DOAC-associated bleeding warrants haemodynamic resuscitation and targeted reversal consideration.
Life-threatening active bleeding requires interrupting anticoagulation and emergency haemostasis.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban.
Additional anticoagulation increases active bleeding and is unsafe.
Severe GI haemorrhage and shock require inpatient resuscitation and definitive care.
pearl: In major DOAC bleeding, stop the drug, stabilise physiology, consider reversal for life-threatening haemorrhage and control the source.
pivot: For minor self-limited bleeding, temporary interruption without reversal may be sufficient depending on risk and timing.

steps: ABCDE, IV access, crossmatch, blood products guided by physiology and bleeding, group and urgent gastro/endoscopy consultation.
Stop apixaban; senior haematology review for factor Xa inhibitor reversal (specific agent or PCC based on availability/indication).
Urgent therapeutic endoscopy when stabilised; PPI if suspected ulcer and other source-specific treatment.
Reassess thromboembolism risk and timing of resuming anticoagulation with specialists.
management.safety: Do not use vitamin K or protamine as routine apixaban reversal; document time of last dose and renal function.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 27-year-old has nausea, jaundice and ALT 1600 U/L after taking multiple cold remedies and analgesics. INR is 2.0 and she is becoming confused; bilirubin is 86 µmol/L. There is no known chronic liver disease.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Advise alcohol avoidance and repeat LFTs in a month.
Treat coagulopathy with routine prophylactic FFP in every patient without assessing bleeding.
Arrange outpatient ultrasound before assessing mental state or paracetamol use.
Give empiric acetylcysteine only after a clearly toxic paracetamol level is confirmed.
Urgently admit to critical-care/liver service, evaluate paracetamol exposure and initiate appropriate N-acetylcysteine without delay.
explanations: INR elevation and encephalopathy indicate acute liver failure needing immediate specialist escalation.
INR tracks synthetic failure; indiscriminate plasma can obscure trends and carries volume risks.
Imaging can help but cannot delay acute liver failure management.
In suspected late/multiple-dose toxicity and liver injury, NAC may be indicated despite uncertain level or timing.
Correct: encephalopathy plus coagulopathy in acute liver injury suggests acute liver failure and potential transplantation needs.
pearl: Acute liver failure is encephalopathy with significant coagulopathy after acute hepatic injury, regardless of transaminase magnitude.
pivot: Isolated raised ALT with preserved INR and normal cognition may be assessed less urgently depending on cause.

steps: ABCDE, blood glucose, INR/PT, hepatic panel, venous gas, creatinine and frequent neuro checks.
Start NAC when suspected paracetamol injury or as advised by liver/toxicology service; check drug formulations and total cumulative dose.
Viral, autoimmune, medication/toxicology testing and Doppler imaging while consulting hepatology.
Discuss transplant-centre transfer, manage hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema risk and organ dysfunction.
management.safety: Do not give sedatives indiscriminately or delay transplant-centre contact for full aetiological confirmation.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 29-year-old at 20 weeks has an asymptomatic midstream urine culture showing 10^5 CFU/mL group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy and a normal renal scan.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate plan?
options: Give only intrapartum antibiotics and leave present bacteriuria untreated.
Treat with an appropriate pregnancy-safe antibiotic now and plan intrapartum GBS prophylaxis.
Ignore the culture because asymptomatic UTI is harmless in pregnancy.
Give lifelong penicillin suppression after delivery.
Recommend elective Caesarean at 37 weeks solely because GBS grew in urine.
explanations: Current high-count bacteriuria warrants antepartum treatment.
Correct: significant GBS bacteriuria merits treatment and is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis even if follow-up culture clears.
High-count asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy increases pyelonephritis risk and warrants treatment.
Routine lifelong suppression is not indicated.
GBS bacteriuria alone does not mandate Caesarean delivery.
pearl: Any GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy signals heavy colonisation and need for intrapartum prophylaxis; treat current ASB according to colony count and policy.
pivot: GBS detected only on a late rectovaginal swab with no UTI is managed by intrapartum prophylaxis rather than antepartum eradication.

steps: Confirm bacterial count, culture sensitivity, symptoms and antibiotic allergy.
Give appropriate pregnancy-compatible antibiotic course and confirm urine clearance according to local protocol.
Document GBS bacteriuria prominently for labour prophylaxis.
Review recurrent UTI symptoms and renal risk.
management.safety: Follow local antimicrobial sensitivity because GBS macrolide/clindamycin resistance varies.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 3-year-old develops reduced urine output and pallor five days after bloody diarrhoea. Hb is 76 g/L, platelets 58 ×10^9/L and creatinine 190 µmol/L. Blood film has schistocytes. Coagulation profile is normal.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give routine antimotility drugs and antibiotics for presumed uncomplicated gastroenteritis.
Arrange admission under paediatric nephrology for supportive fluid, electrolyte, blood pressure and renal care.
Perform emergency splenectomy because haemolysis and thrombocytopenia indicate ITP.
Initiate chronic oral steroid treatment as first-line for all diarrhoea-associated HUS.
Give prophylactic platelet transfusions to normalise counts before review.
explanations: After suspected shiga-toxin infection, antimotility treatment and some antibiotics may worsen risk; now there is HUS.
Correct: typical shiga-toxin HUS is primarily managed supportively while monitoring kidney failure and haemolysis.
This is microangiopathic haemolysis with AKI, not isolated ITP.
Routine steroids do not reverse shiga-toxin HUS.
Platelets are generally reserved for significant bleeding/procedures, not routine correction.
pearl: The triad of microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and AKI after bloody diarrhoea suggests typical HUS.
pivot: Atypical complement-mediated HUS may require targeted complement inhibition after specialist investigation.

steps: Assess hydration versus fluid overload, BP, urine output, ECG and neurological status.
Careful fluid/electrolyte balance, avoid nephrotoxins, manage hypertension and dialyse for indications.
Red-cell transfusion when symptomatic/severe; avoid routine platelet transfusion.
Serial FBC/creatinine and stool shiga-toxin testing when indicated.
management.safety: Monitor for hyperkalaemia, hypertensive encephalopathy and seizures.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 70-year-old with a knee replacement three months ago has rapidly increasing joint pain, swelling and temperature 38.4°C. CRP is 172 mg/L; ultrasound shows an effusion and radiograph reveals no fracture. He remains haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which is the BEST next step?
options: Remove the prosthesis in ED without cultures or specialist planning.
Start intra-articular corticosteroid for presumed postoperative synovitis.
Arrange routine annual review as swelling is common after replacement.
Urgent orthopaedic assessment and sterile joint aspiration with blood cultures before targeted treatment where safe.
Give a one-day oral antibiotic course without further assessment.
explanations: Prosthetic source control requires orthopaedic expertise and surgery planning.
Steroid injection risks worsening infection.
Fever, effusion and high inflammation require urgent evaluation.
Correct: suspected prosthetic joint infection needs microbiological diagnosis and coordinated surgical/antibiotic strategy.
Short therapy may sterilise cultures and inadequately treat biofilm infection.
pearl: Prosthetic joint infection differs from native septic arthritis because biofilm and implant retention/exchange strategies matter.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable/septic, start broad IV antibiotics promptly after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: Assess fever, wound/drainage and joint function; urgent orthopaedic/infection referral.
Blood cultures and aseptic joint aspiration for cell count, cultures and crystals when stable.
Specialist-directed IV antibiotics and debridement/implant-retention or revision strategy by onset/stability.
Monitor inflammatory response and prolonged organism-specific therapy.
management.safety: Avoid starting antibiotics before necessary cultures when stable, but never delay in shock.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A healthy 43-year-old without family history asks for annual mammograms after a friend was diagnosed with breast cancer. She has average baseline risk, no breast symptoms and lives in a country with a population screening start age above 43.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Recommend breast MRI annually to every average-risk woman.
Order serum CA15-3 as an alternative cancer screening test.
Refuse to discuss screening because she is younger than programme entry age.
Discuss personalised risk, programme guidance, false positives, overdiagnosis and her values before deciding.
Promise annual imaging will prevent all future breast-cancer deaths.
explanations: MRI is generally reserved for selected high-risk situations and increases false positives.
Tumour markers do not replace validated breast screening.
Informed discussion of risk, benefits and harms remains appropriate.
Correct: screening decisions should reflect evidence, age/risk and informed patient preference.
Screening can reduce some breast-cancer mortality but has false positives and overdiagnosis; no guarantee exists.
pearl: Population screening depends on net benefit in an age/risk group; earlier testing can increase harms without comparable benefit.
pivot: A pathogenic high-risk mutation or strong pedigree requires formal risk assessment and earlier tailored surveillance.

steps: Concerns, symptoms, family history, previous breast findings and expectations.
Absolute potential benefits, false positives, unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis; compare local screening intervals.
Shared plan and breast-awareness advice, with diagnostic imaging if new symptoms appear.
Review eligibility and preferences as the patient enters the screening age range, develops new breast symptoms or identifies hereditary risk.
management.safety: Never call a symptomatic breast lump 'screening'; it requires diagnostic assessment.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 44-year-old notices a changing 9 mm pigmented back lesion with asymmetric borders, colour variegation and a new nodular component. His mother had melanoma. There is no infection or bleeding.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Freeze the lesion with liquid nitrogen and reassess appearance.
Reassure because lesion is under 1 cm.
Perform complete excisional biopsy with narrow clinical margins or urgent specialist referral for appropriate biopsy.
Shave a superficial portion only without assessing depth.
Prescribe topical corticosteroid for four weeks.
explanations: Cryotherapy destroys histological architecture and can delay diagnosis.
Melanoma can be smaller than 6 mm; evolution and atypia matter.
Correct: changing ABCDE features require histopathologic diagnosis with accurate Breslow staging.
Partial superficial sampling may impair Breslow thickness assessment; biopsy choice requires guideline alignment.
A suspicious melanocytic lesion is not a rash to trial steroids.
pearl: Evolution, asymmetry, border irregularity and colour variation are high-risk melanoma signs; histology determines staging.
pivot: A stable symmetric uniformly coloured nevus without concerning features may be photographed/monitored under appropriate dermoscopy review.

steps: ABCDE changes, personal/family history and full skin examination.
Excisional biopsy with narrow diagnostic margins when feasible, or dermatology referral for complex sites.
Histological Breslow thickness and ulceration guide wider excision and sentinel node discussion.
Sun protection and skin surveillance for patient/family.
management.safety: Do not destroy suspicious lesions without histology.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 32-year-old ten days after Caesarean delivery develops sudden pleuritic pain, severe breathlessness and collapse. HR 138/min, BP 72/40 mmHg, SpO2 84% and the right ventricle is severely dilated on bedside echocardiography. There is no major bleeding currently.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate approach?
options: Begin oral apixaban and review symptoms at four hours.
Send her alone for an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram before any resuscitation.
Give two litres of IV crystalloid rapidly without reassessment to fill the right ventricle.
Activate resuscitation and senior PE response; support circulation and consider immediate reperfusion after bleeding-risk assessment.
Prescribe empirical oral antibiotics to cover pneumonia while awaiting a D-dimer.
explanations: An oral drug alone is insufficient for shock from a likely massive PE; critical-care and reperfusion decisions are urgent.
Unstable transfer for imaging can precipitate arrest; stabilise and assess reperfusion urgently.
Large fluid loads can worsen RV failure and cardiac output in PE; fluids must be cautiously titrated.
Correct: obstructive shock with high-probability PE needs ABC support and urgent specialist reperfusion consideration.
The presentation and RV findings suggest high-risk PE; D-dimer cannot safely direct management in shock.
pearl: Postpartum PE can present as obstructive shock; a normal or modest D-dimer is not a safe exclusion test in this setting.
pivot: If stable with lower probability, use an appropriate structured diagnostic pathway and definitive imaging rather than emergency reperfusion.

steps: Call ED/anaesthesia/ICU and obstetric teams; high-flow oxygen when hypoxaemic, ECG, IV access, close haemodynamic monitoring.
Carefully assess fluid response; use vasopressors as required for persistent hypotension and avoid unnecessary transfer.

Urgent CTPA if stable for imaging; if too unstable, multidisciplinary decision based on bedside findings and probability; anticoagulation and reperfusion according to bleeding risk and service availability.
Monitor haemorrhage and haemodynamics, assess provoking factors, counsel on anticoagulation compatible with breastfeeding under specialist advice.
management.safety: Recent surgery and postpartum haemorrhage risks materially affect choice of thrombolysis versus catheter/surgical alternatives.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 2-year-old has a barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate intercostal recession and agitation. He is pink with SpO2 96%, is speaking in short phrases, and no choking event occurred.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV antibiotics because croup is almost always bacterial.
Keep the child calm, give oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, then observe for recurrence.
Examine the oropharynx forcefully with a tongue depressor before treating.
Discharge immediately once stridor improves after nebulised adrenaline.
Give salbutamol via spacer as first-line because any stridor is bronchospasm.
explanations: Typical croup is viral; routine antibiotics provide no benefit.
Correct: stridor at rest indicates moderate/severe croup requiring corticosteroid and inhaled adrenaline with observation.
Unnecessary distress can worsen upper airway obstruction; assess non-invasively and keep child calm.
Adrenaline effect can wear off; observe the child for recurrent stridor, particularly after moderate/severe presentation.
Stridor is upper-airway obstruction; beta agonists do not treat subglottic oedema.
pearl: Croup is upper-airway oedema: dexamethasone provides sustained benefit; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid but temporary relief.
pivot: If drooling, toxic appearance, tripod posture or difficult swallowing dominate, consider epiglottitis/deep neck infection and call expert airway help.

steps: Keep the child with parent, avoid painful procedures until necessary, monitor severity and oxygenation.
Give dexamethasone per local croup protocol and nebulised adrenaline when stridor at rest or significant respiratory distress.
Observe after adrenaline for recurrence; seek senior/anaesthetic support for exhaustion, cyanosis, reduced consciousness or poor response.
management.safety: Do not perform throat examination that agitates a child with suspected dangerous upper-airway obstruction.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 46-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis and immunosuppressive therapy has a hot swollen knee, fever 38.6 °C and cannot bear weight. BP 120/70 mmHg. Bedside ultrasound shows a large effusion.
ask: What is the BEST initial approach?
options: Arrange urgent aseptic synovial aspiration and blood cultures, then empiric IV antibiotics and orthopaedic drainage planning.
Prescribe oral doxycycline alone and reassess the swollen knee tomorrow.
Start intra-articular corticosteroid immediately because RA flare is most likely.
Order MRI before obtaining a joint aspirate.
Treat with oral NSAIDs and arrange rheumatology review in two weeks.
explanations: Correct: aspiration confirms infection and guides microbiology, while prompt antibiotics and source control protect joint and patient.
Empiric outpatient oral therapy is inadequate for a suspected infected native joint.
Steroid injection into an infected joint can worsen infection; septic arthritis must be excluded.
MRI may be useful in complications but should not delay aspiration, cultures and treatment.
Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage rapidly and needs emergency assessment.
pearl: Septic arthritis is a joint emergency: aspiration before antibiotics is ideal if stable, but do not delay antimicrobials in sepsis.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable, start antibiotics immediately after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: Assess sepsis, give analgesia, contact orthopaedics, blood cultures and labs.
Aseptic joint aspirate for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals; crystals do not exclude concurrent infection.
Empiric IV antibiotics guided by local resistance and risk factors; urgent washout/drainage as required.
Tailor therapy to culture, repeat assessment for ongoing infection and rehabilitation when safe.
management.safety: Immunosuppression can blunt fever or inflammatory signs; maintain a low threshold for septic arthritis.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 43-year-old with obesity presents with tiredness and thirst. HbA1c is 82 mmol/mol (9.7%) and fasting glucose 13 mmol/L. He is not acidotic, has no ketones or catabolic weight loss, and renal function is normal.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Explain the diagnosis, assess complications/cardiovascular risk, start lifestyle support and pharmacotherapy with early reassessment.
Diagnose type 1 diabetes automatically because he reports thirst and fatigue.
Commence IV insulin infusion and admit everyone with HbA1c above 80 mmol/mol.
Recommend six months of dietary change only and avoid medication until HbA1c exceeds 11%.
Discharge without follow-up if the urine ketone test is negative.
explanations: Correct: significant hyperglycaemia needs a structured treatment plan, not lifestyle advice alone; drug choice is individualised.
Symptoms alone do not distinguish diabetes subtype; evaluate phenotype, ketones and autoimmune features when clinically indicated.
IV insulin is for metabolic emergencies or selected severe inpatient situations, not all stable type 2 diabetes.
Marked symptomatic hyperglycaemia deserves timely pharmacological intervention and close follow-up.
Absence of DKA does not remove long-term organ and vascular risk requiring treatment.
pearl: New type 2 diabetes management includes lifestyle, individualised glucose-lowering drugs, cardiovascular/renal risk and retinal/foot screening.
pivot: Marked ketosis, rapid weight loss, dehydration or acidosis raises concern for insulin deficiency/DKA and changes urgency.

steps: Confirm glucose pattern, symptoms and ketones; renal function, BP, lipids, urine ACR, eye/foot screening and cardiovascular risk.
Diet/activity support and pharmacotherapy, commonly metformin if suitable; consider early combination or insulin for very high symptomatic glucose, guided by comorbidities.
Home glucose review, adherence, education and hypoglycaemia safety when applicable; titrate treatment within weeks.
Discuss smoking cessation, vaccinations, BP/lipids and kidney/cardiovascular protective agents when indicated.
management.safety: Do not start metformin in significant metabolic acidosis or unstable renal failure; selection depends on eGFR and risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones has corrected calcium 2.86 mmol/L and an inappropriately elevated PTH. Renal function is stable and she has no severe dehydration.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate long-term management discussion?
options: Order thyroidectomy because the high PTH is from thyroid follicular cells.
Give lifelong phosphate supplements as definitive therapy.
Treat every patient with emergency haemodialysis for calcium above 2.8.
Consider referral for parathyroidectomy because symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism meets surgical criteria.
